# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read the follow-up carefully and checked its numbers. It is the most informative document in the set. It answers questions the earlier papers left open:
- Unrecorded work is now measured with system logs, and the gain survives.
- The meetings hypothesis gets a registered test.
- The meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies turn out to be all uncontrolled and based on scheduled hours, as I suspected in my review of it.

Its rebuttals of both "entirely an artifact" and "no sign of decay" are justified. The main problems are a misleading comparison in the Summary, contamination of the control group that the authors report but don't analyse, and a mediation analysis that is less independent and less precise than presented.

## Arithmetic checks

These figures check out:
- Varden, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- Varden, system logs: 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- Halden subset hours: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, or −13.4%.
- Halden subset per-hour gain: 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- Counter staffing: restoring output with per-employee output at 0.886 needs about 1 / 0.886, or 12.9% more staff. That matches the county's "12% more staff". The 9% rise in cost per contact implies that staff are about three-quarters of cost per contact. State that assumption.

## Major issues

**1. The Summary compares figures from different hours measures.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data" puts a timesheet figure next to a log figure. The like-for-like comparison, given in the body, is **12.5% → 9.8%**, a decline of about a fifth. Section 5's "about a quarter" matches neither comparison: 12.5 → 9.8 is −22%, and 12.5 → 8.5 is −32%. Give both figures in the Summary.

Also, the two intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4, and +4.6 to +15.2). Report a CI for the *change*. The decline may not be statistically distinguishable from zero. "Consistent with some fading" is fair wording; the Summary's "has therefore declined" is stronger than the evidence.

**2. The "meeting audit" contaminates the control group, and the 24-month estimate isn't adjusted for it.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15. From then on, the control arm partly received the mechanism being tested. This shrinks the difference between treated and controls, which has two consequences:
- The 24-month estimate is probably biased **downward**.
- Part of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control offices improving, not the treated offices fading.

The audits may also be spillover from the trial itself. To check:
- re-estimate excluding the two offices;
- estimate separately for months 9–15 and 15–24.

The control-arm averages also don't reconcile. If two of seven offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control average should fall by about 0.6 hours. The reported fall is from 7.2 to 7.0. That requires the other five offices to have *increased* meeting time by about half an hour each. Report the figures for each office.

**3. The mediation CIs are probably too narrow.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not add independent observations. There are still 7 treated and 7 control offices, and repeated months within an office are correlated. With 14 clusters, clustered or bootstrapped intervals need the corrections for small numbers of clusters that I raised in my review of the nine-month report. The same applies to the main per-hour CI (+3.4 to +13.8). Its lower bound clears zero "by a clear margin" only if the standard errors are trustworthy. State the inference method.

**4. The registered test guards against analytic flexibility, but it is not a replication.** It was registered at month 11, after the exploratory result, and uses **the same seven treated offices** that generated the hypothesis, over months that overlap the exploratory window. That is a real improvement. But Varga & Holm's concern, that a hypothesis drawn from seven offices may not hold elsewhere, is not fully answered by retesting it in those same offices. "Confirms" in the Summary should be "supports". The genuine test would be a different setting, or a trial arm that reorganises meetings without cutting hours, which the authors themselves note is missing.

**5. Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected **only in month six**; there was no baseline, which is why I said "offices that cut meetings most" could not be computed. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2). If they were recovered from historical calendars, say so and describe how complete they are. Their reliability affects the mediation result directly.

**6. Define the hours denominator. The answer changes what the mediation result means.** "Active log-in time on the case-management system" could mean either of two things:
- *Case-working time only, excluding meetings.* Then a meetings effect operates through focus or fragmentation, which is a substantive finding. But then log hours shouldn't fall by 11%. Treated non-meeting time fell only about 3–4% relative to control: roughly 30.5 → 29.5 hours, against a small rise in control.
- *Total working time, including meetings.* Then cutting meetings raises output per hour partly by simple reallocation, since freed meeting time becomes case time. A rough accounting check:
  - output fell 3.4%, and non-meeting time fell about 4%;
  - so output per non-meeting hour is roughly **unchanged** (≈ +0.6%);
  - reallocation alone would therefore explain nearly the **whole** per-hour gain, not 47%.

Either way, the 47% needs reconciling with this simple accounting. Report the gain per non-meeting hour directly.

## Halden subset

- **The Summary's framing of reversions doesn't hold.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations", but one was a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**. The meta-analysis would code that as discretionary work. It is a genuine counterexample to the split between discretionary and coverage-bound work, which may be too clean. External deadlines can make discretionary work behave as if tied to presence. Say this plainly; it is interesting.
- **Survivorship compounds.** As well as the three reversions, 9 of 23 organisations didn't provide data. Excluding reverters, whose output was 88–91, mechanically raises the 96.8. The authors' "upper bound" caveat is right. Also report a figure including reverters' output at the point of reversion.
- **Check the baseline.** The continuing subset's baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the 27-organisation average in Varga & Holm. Confirm it is the 11 organisations' own figure.
- **The attrition finding goes unanswered.** Varga & Holm reported from the microdata that 7 of the 9 withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, contradicting the working paper. With a Halden author among the co-authors, this report is the natural place to acknowledge or correct that. It answers the re-analysis's other claims, but not this one.

## Smaller points

- **Backlogs and cost.** These are still not reported for case-processing. Two years is long enough for backlog growth to show. The county costed the counter arm; do the same for case-processing, including any overtime.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still doesn't adjust for fewer scheduled days, if rotas reduced days worked.
- **Quality outcomes.** The appeal overturn rate (3.2% v 3.0%) is now past the appeal lag, which is good. It still has no CI.
- **The unplanned observation.** It is appropriately hedged. Its +4.1% is an uncontrolled before-and-after change in two offices whose control group is the same trial. Treat it purely as a hypothesis for a reorganisation-only arm.

## Updated synthesis

With this report, the evidence across all five documents looks like this:

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work, rigorous measures | **~8.5–10% at 24 months** (one randomised trial); somewhat below the 9-month figure, possibly partly because the control arm also cut meetings |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly down (~−3%), CI includes zero |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker falls ~9–11%; service worsens; restoring it costs ~9–13% more; Varden abandoned it |
| Inflation in uncontrolled pilots | Roughly doubles the apparent gain |
| Durability | Modest fading over two years in one trial; neither "entirely novelty" nor "no decay" holds |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the leading candidate, possibly explaining most of the gain; fatigue contributes less; neither is established independently of these seven offices |
| Open question | Could reorganisation without cutting hours capture most of the gain? Untested |

The most useful next study would be a trial with three arms: reduced hours, meeting reorganisation alone, and control. That design directly tests whether cutting hours is what makes reorganisation happen and stick.

I can draft referee comments for this report, or turn the table above into a short synthesis note.
